The goal is to encrypt in-memory data and process it inside secure enclaves, which are protected
environments that restrict access to authorized code. Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs),
such as Intel SGX and AMD SEV, enable these enclaves using hardware-based security features.
Confidential computing is a broader paradigm that encompasses TEEs and other technologies to
protect data while it is in use—complementing encryption at rest and in transit. Azure includes
several services that are associated with confidential computing. You can visit this link to get
an exhaustive list: https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/confidential-compute.
Let’s now look at different ways to maintain data integrity.
Preserving data integrity
Data access can be controlled using Azure Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). All Azure services—
whether data-centric or not—generate activity logs that capture control plane operations. These
logs can be ingested by Azure Sentinel or any other SIEM solution for comprehensive monitoring.
For data plane activities, certain services, such as Azure SQL, provide dedicated audit logs.

90928.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90928.heading: Chapter 9 333
90928.content:
Chapter 9 333
To safeguard against accidental deletions or modifications, Azure offers features such as soft delete,
purge protection, and versioning for some services. Cosmos DB includes a change feed mechanism
that tracks operations performed on data. Additionally, Azure SQL and Synapse support dynamic
data masking, allowing sensitive information to be obfuscated at runtime. Additionally, backup
solutions such as a Backup vault allow us to take immutable backups.
In summary, it’s essential to verify which features are supported by the data services you intend
to use and to enable data protection-specific features.
Next, let’s talk about data governance.
Ensuring proper data governance
Selecting the appropriate encryption model and mitigating possible integrity issues is an import -
ant part of governance, but it’s only one piece of the puzzle. Equally critical is implementing a
robust data classification framework to differentiate between general data, sensitive information,
and intellectual property. This classification helps determine the level of protection required
and guides encryption, access control, and auditing policies accordingly. Microsoft Purview has
evolved into a unified service that delivers a consolidated experience for data governance. While
it is deeply integrated with Microsoft 365, especially in the areas of information protection and
data loss prevention, our focus here will be limited to its Azure-specific capabilities and how
Purview can help with data governance within the Azure ecosystem.
The Microsoft Purview Data Map is one of the core components to integrate Azure data services
with Microsoft Purview. For the Data Map to show up in the Purview portal (https://purview.
microsoft.com/), you must have a Purview account created in Azure.
Once you have a Purview account in Azure, the Data Map component will be available in the
Purview portal. From there, you can organize a hierarchy of collections and subcollections to deal
with the various data sources in an organized way, as shown in Figure 9.3.
Figure 9.3 – Organizing Data Map collections and subcollections
Security Architecture 334
All the collections are bound to a domain, and multiple domains can be created.
We can assign permissions at each level, which helps delegate data management operations to
different teams. Figure 9.3 illustrates a sample hierarchy based on resource types, but you could
also structure it by location or any other attribute relevant to your organization.
Using the Data Map, you can scan Azure data sources, allowing Microsoft Purview to automat -
ically discover and classify sensitive data. This provides comprehensive visibility across your
data landscape.
We can connect the Data Map to a variety of data sources, such as Blob Storage, Data Lake, Cosmos

90929.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90929.heading: Chapter 9 333
90929.content:
DB, Azure SQL, Data Explorer, Databricks, and Synapse. It also has connectors for Fabric and AWS.
Figure 9.4 shows how we can connect the Data Map to Azure Blob Storage:
Figure 9.4 – Data Map connected to Azure Blob Storage
Figure 9.4 illustrates a storage account that has public access disabled. Microsoft Purview connects
to it using managed private endpoints. As a best practice, it is recommended to use user-assigned
managed identities to access target data sources. This approach supports the principle of least
privilege by ensuring each identity is granted only the specific permissions needed on the cor -
responding data source.

90930.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90930.heading: Chapter 9 335
90930.content:
Chapter 9 335
With this setup in place, we performed a scan on our storage account, which contained random
PDF invoices. As shown in Figure 9.5, Purview successfully identified sensitive financial informa -
tion, including bank account numbers, through its automated classification capabilities.
Figure 9.5 – Automatic classification
We used the default scanning ruleset for a storage account, but we can create our own rulesets.
This example shows how useful Purview can be to keep control over data stored in Azure. Purview
shines even more with well-structured data, such as relational databases.
This concludes our section on data security. Now, let’s turn our attention to identity—the primary
security layer in the cloud.
Security Architecture 336
Zooming in on identity
The identity landscape in Azure is very broad. Figure 9.6 depicts its most important parts:
Figure 9.6 – Identity landscape
Let’s now dive into specific sections, starting with IDAM and CIAM.
Introducing the main solutions used for IDAM and CIAM
Entra ID serves as the foundation for IDAM across the Microsoft ecosystem. Every Azure subscrip -
tion is associated with an Entra ID instance, referred to as a tenant. Corporate users, including
employees and collaborators, have identities in Entra ID to carry out their daily tasks. In many
organizations, an on-premises Active Directory remains in use and is synchronized with Entra ID
via Entra Connect. While federating Entra ID with Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)
was once common, this approach is now discouraged due to the increasing centrality of Entra ID
over the past decade. AD FS was mostly used to establish identity federation with partners and
integrate with on-premises, but this has now shifted to Entra ID. Today, Entra ID stands as the
core component of any IDAM strategy.

90931.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90931.heading: Chapter 9 337
90931.content:
Chapter 9 337
In the realm of Customer Identity and Access Management (CIAM), Entra ID is often used to
provide external or customer access to Microsoft 365 through B2B guest invitations, also known
as B2B collaboration, and to allow external partners/customers to access organizational assets
through federation. However, Microsoft positions Entra External ID, formerly Azure B2C, as its
dedicated CIAM solution, designed from the ground up to support customer authentication and
authorization. Entra External ID supports advanced authentication workflows and includes social
identity providers such as Facebook and Google out of the box.
Niche players such as Auth0/Okta and Ping/ForgeRock are among the most advanced solutions in
the CIAM world. ForgeRock has an impressive offering and can accommodate nearly any authen -
tication workflow. It also integrates with HSMs (Azure Dedicated HSM or your own on-premises
HSM), which is particularly useful to sign JWT tokens and Security Assertion Markup Language
(SAML) assertions since the private keys used to sign such tokens never leave the boundaries of
the HSM.
Introducing authentication, authorization, and Conditional
Access policies
The terms authentication and authorization are often confused—partly because certain features
straddle both domains.
Authentication is the process whereby a user submits credentials to an identity provider, which
then verifies them. Once successfully validated, the user is signed in.
Authorization determines whether a user or application has permission to access a particular
resource. It’s the responsibility of the resource server to allow or deny access.
This distinction can become blurred with features such as Conditional Access, which intersects
both processes.
For instance, during user sign-in, Conditional Access might prompt for Multi-Factor Authen -
tication (MFA) based on specific conditions (such as login attempts from unfamiliar locations),
but it can also serve as an access gatekeeper—deciding, for example, whether a user can enter
the Azure portal depending on preconfigured rules. Blocking access is more part of the authori -
zation realm than the authentication one. Conditional Access can be seen as the policy engine of
a zero-trust security model that makes decisions based on signals received from devices, users,
networks, and locations.
All of this can contribute to confusion between authentication and authorization.
Security Architecture 338
The Identity Protection feature protects against malicious authentication activities. Figure 9.7
illustrates the different features made available by Identity Protection:
Figure 9.7 – Identity Protection

90932.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90932.heading: Chapter 9 339
90932.content:
Chapter 9 339
Identity Protection is mostly useful for detecting three types of risks: user, sign-in, and workload
identity risks.
A user risk means that the user might have been compromised. A sign-in risk is identified while
the user signs in. A workload identity risk means that a service principal (non-human user) might
have been compromised.
By combining risk detection with CAPs, we can prevent potentially compromised users or appli -
cations from accessing specific resources. CAPs allow us to define powerful rules. For example,
very common rules that can be defined are the following:
• Triggering MFA when accessing specific resources
• Location-based policies, such as either requiring MFA or denying/granting access based
on the user’s location
• Requiring full re-authentication for risk-based policies
• Enforcing the use of corporate devices only
• Triggering MFA if a low/medium sign-in risk is identified
• Blocking access in case a high user, sign-in, or workload identity risk is identified
All these policies typically end up with either blocking or granting access, or triggering MFA.
For example, if you run a business in a specific country or a handful of countries, you may block
all locations except the ones you’re active in. The following is a real-world-inspired policy that
had to comply with the following rules:
• Access to all apps except Azure DevOps and Microsoft Azure Management was blocked
when coming from outside of Belgium and the Netherlands
• Locations such as India and Morocco were allowed for the two exempted apps because
some specific tasks were outsourced
Security Architecture 340
These rules correspond to the policy illustrated in Figure 9.8:
Figure 9.8 – Blocking access from non-whitelisted countries with Conditional Access
As you can see in Figure 9.8, there is also the possibility to enable the policy in report mode. This
is particularly convenient to observe the behavior of a policy once activated and make sure you
didn’t make any configuration mistakes, as it directly impacts the login experience and may cause
trouble for end users. Another possibility is to have a non-production tenant (a separate instance
of Entra ID) where you can test those policies.

90933.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90933.heading: Chapter 9 341
90933.content:
Chapter 9 341
An additional authentication-related feature is Smart Lockout, which helps prevent brute-force
attacks by only locking the account after a configurable number of failed attempts, and by im -
posing a configurable time interval across login attempts.
Lastly, Entra ID has a few passwordless options and integrates seamlessly with FIDO2/passkeys,
the Microsoft Authenticator app, as well as Temporary Access Pass (TAP) and QR code-based
authentication. TAP allows you to register passwordless authentication methods.
In terms of authorization, Entra ID has directory-specific roles, such as Application Developer,
Application Administrator, and Global Administrator, which all allow you to manage and config -
ure Entra ID. For any Azure-related resources, we rely on Azure RBAC, which features hundreds
of roles. It is important to consider the Azure hierarchy that we described in Chapter 2, Solution
Architecture, since it is where we apply RBAC permissions and policies. We’ll tackle other autho -
rization-specific aspects in the next section.
Introducing common protocols such as OIDC, OAuth 2.0,
and SAML
SAML is a widely recognized legacy protocol that remains in active use today, particularly in fed -
eration scenarios. However, cloud-native applications typically rely on OAuth 2.0 and OpenID
Connect (OIDC), and newer federation implementations are increasingly adopting OIDC. As such,
our focus will be exclusively on OAuth 2.0 and OIDC. That said, it’s important to acknowledge
that SAML continues to play a role and is expected to persist for the foreseeable future.
Both OAuth 2.0 and OIDC are international standards and are not specific to Azure. In this section,
we will examine how Entra ID supports these protocols, noting that its implementation does not
fully align with the specifications in all aspects.
Security Architecture 342
Before diving deeper into endpoints, tokens, and authorization flows, it’s important to first un -
derstand the key actors involved when using OIDC with Entra ID.
Figure 9.9 – OIDC actors with Entra ID
Figure 9.9 shows three main actors:
• The identity and authorization server: In Figure 9.9, Entra ID plays both roles. Note
that it is rather common to split those roles into two distinct services. For example, you
may use Entra External ID for authentication and Keycloak or Duende for authorization.
• The business application: This can be anything that uses either a public or confidential
client application. We’ll explain these different types of applications later. In any case, the
business service will have to use a client application for which a corresponding applica -
tion object exists in Entra ID. This requires the registration of the client application prior
to its use. In Entra ID, we can grant permissions over resources to the client application.

90934.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90934.heading: Chapter 9 341
90934.content:
• The resource server: This can, for example, be a backend service that is exposed as an
API. This resource server must have a corresponding resource identifier in Entra ID. This
is typically achieved by registering an application that represents the resource server and
that exposes an API. We can optionally expose custom roles and scopes. The resource server
must perform the token validation to ensure the calling client is legitimate.

90935.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90935.heading: Chapter 9 343
90935.content:
Chapter 9 343
Note that Entra ID allows us to use a single application object to represent both the client and
the resource, but this is rather considered bad practice to club them and would only make sense
when the client and the resource share the same lifecycle.
Whenever a business application requests a token, Entra ID verifies that both the client applica -
tion and the target resource (resource server) are registered and recognized. It also ensures that
the request complies with the specific requirements of the OAuth flow being used by the calling
application.
Now that the fundamentals are in place, let’s explore the broader OIDC landscape.
Figure 9.10 illustrates the vast world of OIDC, which is a layer on top of OAuth 2.0:
Figure 9.10 – OIDC map
Important note
To have a better view of this map, you can download the PDF file available at https://
github.com/PacktPublishing/The-Azure-Cloud-Native-Architecture-
Mapbook-Second-Edition/blob/main/Chapter09/maps/oidc.pdf
Security Architecture 344
Figure 9.10 provides a generic overview of OIDC’s capabilities. It includes warning symbols to draw
attention to specific considerations or limitations relevant to Entra ID, which will be detailed in
the following sections.
The five dimensions we’re going to explore are shown in Figure 9.11:
Figure 9.11 – OIDC dimensions
Let’s start with the Endpoints section.
Understanding OIDC endpoints and mapping them to Entra ID
Any OIDC interaction must go through one of the endpoints illustrated in Figure 9.12:

90936.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90936.heading: Chapter 9 345
90936.content:
Chapter 9 345
Figure 9.12 – Entra ID endpoints for OIDC
The Discovery endpoint is a well-known URL that exposes configuration metadata necessary for
clients to integrate with Entra ID. The endpoint looks as follows:
https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant>/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration.
This endpoint returns a document that outlines Entra ID’s capabilities. It essentially serves as a
directory of the available endpoints and includes the location of the public keys—exposed via
the jwks_uri attribute—that can be used to verify the signatures of tokens issued by Entra ID.
We’ll come back to token validation practices later on.
The Authorization endpoint handles things such as user consent, meaning when a client ap -
plication has requested access to a resource on behalf of a user (resource owner). Upon user
consent, it typically returns an authorization code, which can be reused by the client for further
token acquisition. This allows a client application to interact with a resource on your behalf. In
Entra ID, we usually skip the user consent by letting an administrator consent on behalf of the
entire organization.
Security Architecture 346
The Token endpoint is used by client applications to request all types of tokens, among which
are refresh tokens, which we will explain in the next section. When a human user is involved,
the first step is usually to first leverage the authorization endpoint, then connect to the token
endpoint, and exchange the authorization code for an access token. When the client application
needs a token for itself (as an app with no user involved), it typically requests the access token
directly from the token endpoint.
The Introspection endpoint doesn’t exist in Entra ID. It is linked to reference tokens, which we
will explain in the next section. It’s an important limitation of Entra.
The Revocation endpoint is typically used to revoke both refresh and reference tokens, but in
the case of Entra ID, it can only revoke refresh tokens.
The Device Authorization endpoint is used in situations where the client device, such as a smart
TV, doesn’t have a (decent) browser or UI that allows for an easy experience. The user authen -
ticates and can enter a device code sent by Entra ID using another device than the one that is
originally requesting access.
Last but not least, the UserInfo endpoint allows client applications to retrieve additional infor -
mation about the logged-in user.
Be aware that other SAML-specific endpoints are also exposed by Entra ID. Now, let’s look at the
different token types and highlight some other Entra ID limitations.
Understanding token types, lifetime, revocation, and Entra ID
limitations
We already slightly introduced token types in Chapter 6, Developing and Designing Applications
with Azure, but we’ll provide a broader coverage in this section. Let’s start by exploring the dif -

90937.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90937.heading: Chapter 9 345
90937.content:
ferent token types.
Figure 9.13 illustrates the different token types that exist in OIDC:

90938.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90938.heading: Chapter 9 347
90938.content:
Chapter 9 347
Figure 9.13 – Token types
Here is an explanation of the four token types:
• ID tokens: These contain user-related information. They are mostly used in client applica -
tions, such as Single-Page Applications (SPAs) or mobile apps. ID tokens typically contain
claims such as preferred_name or email. They may also contain a pointer to the groups a
given user belongs to. ID tokens should never be used outside of the business application’s
client interface. In other words, they are not meant to be used for API or resource access.
• Access tokens: These represent a credential issued by an authorization server (for exam -
ple, Entra ID) that allows the client application to access resources, such as custom and
third-party APIs, on behalf of the logged-in user or as an application. With Entra ID, access
tokens are not opaque but self-contained value tokens. This means that any entity in posses -
sion of a valid access token can access the resource for which it was issued, regardless of
how the token was obtained. As an analogy, an access token is like a set of house keys:
you don’t need to be the owner to enter—if you have the keys and know where the house
is, you can get inside. Access tokens cannot be revoked in Entra ID.
Security Architecture 348
It is therefore important to consider their lifetime. It’s worth noting that Entra ID supports
Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) based on the OpenID Continuous Access Evalua -
tion Profile (CAEP), allowing your applications and APIs to respond to critical events such
as password changes or account disablement—provided they are CAE-aware themselves.
More on this here: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/
app-resilience-continuous-access-evaluation.
• Refresh tokens: These are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens on
behalf of the authenticated user. They play a key role in avoiding repeated user authen -
tication when access tokens expire, which is especially beneficial for mobile applications
and browser-based clients. However, due to their extended lifespan and critical role in
maintaining session continuity, exposing refresh tokens in public clients poses significant
security risks. A recommended best practice is to implement the Backend for Frontend
(BFF) pattern (described in the next section), which ensures that all token handling re -
mains on the server side, preventing any type of token from being exposed to the client. A
few Entra ID events (changing password, user disabled, etc.) may revoke existing refresh
tokens depending on whether they are used by confidential or public clients. Adminis -
trators can, however, enforce a refresh token revocation for a given user, which applies
to all client types.
• Reference tokens: These are opaque access tokens and they are not supported in Entra ID.

90939.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90939.heading: Chapter 9 347
90939.content:
They act as a pointer to the authorization server. The benefit of using such tokens is that
they can be revoked at any point in time. The APIs receiving such tokens cannot validate
them directly and must call the authorization server’s introspection endpoint. This type
of endpoint doesn’t exist in Entra ID. Be aware that even if Entra ID did support them,
using this type of token would introduce a performance penalty and would require a
highly scalable authorization server, since it would have to handle many more requests.
Alternatives to Entra ID, such as Duende and Keycloak, support reference tokens. However,
they might be more useful in CIAM scenarios, where you may use Entra External ID for
authentication and Duende or Keycloak for authorization.
It is worth noting that the token lifetime also depends on the scenario and the identity that is
used to request a token. Here are the different types of identities available in Entra ID:

90940.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90940.heading: Chapter 9 349
90940.content:
Chapter 9 349
• Registered applications: This type of object is explicitly registered, either to expose and
secure a custom API or to enable API access for client applications. The registration pro -
cess depends on whether the application is intended for use by a public or a confidential
client. When assigning permissions, we differentiate between delegated and application
permissions. Delegated permissions allow the client application to access a resource
(for example, the Graph API) on behalf of the signed-in user, provided that the user or
an administrator has granted consent. This type of app often requires a client secret or
a client certificate, depending on the chosen authorization flow. Be aware that using a
client certificate is considered more secure but adds some extra constraints for the busi -
ness application using the client app. The token lifetime is one hour by default but can be
modified through specific policies. This type of application also benefits from enterprise
features such as the possibility to restrict its use to specific users and groups and map
group memberships to custom API roles.
• Managed identities: This type of object is provisioned by Azure. In practice, we create
Azure resources that are given either system-assigned or user-assigned managed identities,
which automatically results in the creation of a corresponding service principal in Entra
ID. When these managed identities are used to obtain access tokens, the tokens have a
fixed lifetime of 24 hours. This duration cannot be altered. The reason is that applications
using managed identities do not communicate directly with Entra ID’s token endpoint.
Instead, they interact with a local endpoint provided by Azure on the Azure service (for
example, app service, virtual machine, and so on). This local endpoint caches tokens for
24 hours, and there is no supported policy mechanism to override this behavior. Note that
the use of managed identities is mostly restricted to accessing Azure resources such as an
Azure SQL database or a Service Bus instance. It is technically possible to use managed
identities to consume custom APIs, but it is not so common in practice.
• Workload identity federation through user-assigned identities: This type of identity
allows you to establish trust between an external system, such as AKS or GitHub, and En -
tra ID. The external system becomes a token issuer whose tokens can be exchanged with
Entra ID tokens through federated identities materialized using user-assigned managed
identities. As a consequence, the token lifetime is also 24 hours. As for managed identities,
we typically use federation through user-assigned identities to access Azure resources
and leverage the Azure RBAC model to grant permissions.
• Workload identity federation through app registration: This type of identity allows you

90941.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90941.heading: Chapter 9 349
90941.content:
to establish trust between an external system and Entra ID, but the way they integrate
is through an app registration. As a consequence, the token lifetime defaults to one hour
and can be adjusted using custom policies.
Security Architecture 350
While leveraging both managed identities and workload identities is considered a best practice,
the fixed lifetime of the resulting access tokens can raise concerns. Nevertheless, these types of
identities are widely adopted due to their convenience when accessing Azure-only resources.
Infrastructure as code pipelines do not require direct interaction with Entra ID—they only need
to provision user-assigned identities, which automatically result in corresponding service princi -
pals. In contrast, using app registrations instead of user-assigned identities introduces scalability
challenges; they require direct access to Entra ID and support only up to 20 federated credentials
per application, but one of the greatest benefits is that they can be used with Conditional Access,
unlike the other methods. So, it might be a good option for some specific scenarios.
In Kubernetes environments such as AKS, where hundreds or thousands of Pods may exist, ad -
hering to the least-privilege principle would necessitate a large number of app registrations—an
approach that does not scale effectively.
Grasping the different authorization flows and token acquisition
mechanisms
It is essential to identify which authorization flow is appropriate for each type of application. Many
developers and security professionals lack a clear understanding of how these flows should be
used, which can easily result in security vulnerabilities and the leak of tokens/secrets.
As we highlighted earlier, the notion of public and confidential clients is important. Public cli -
ents are applications that cannot securely store credentials or client secrets. For example, a web
browser can store data in its web storage (session or local storage) but the information is easily
accessible by anyone with access to the device. In the case of a web browser, malicious JavaScript
code can also easily be injected and access that sensitive information. Similarly, mobile apps,
user laptops, and so on are considered public clients as their owner/user can typically extract the
information. It is, therefore, important not to store a shared secret on such devices. An example
of a shared secret might be the secret obtained during the app registration process or an API key,
or even the root key of a storage account.
Conversely, confidential clients are server-side components that can easily store secrets and that
are managed by infrastructure administrators. For example, a custom backend service could store
a secret in Azure Key Vault and pull it at runtime using its managed identity. The secret cannot

90942.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90942.heading: Chapter 9 349
90942.content:
be seen directly by the end user.
The type of authorization flow we can use depends on the type of client used by the business
application. Technically, there is nothing preventing the use of a confidential client on an end
user device.

90943.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90943.heading: Chapter 9 351
90943.content:
Chapter 9 351
For example, you could embed a client ID and client secret in a mobile app package and use it from
a mobile device. However, such credentials could easily be extracted through package inspection
or traffic capture. It is, therefore, the responsibility of security analysts and architects to assess
and mitigate the associated risks.
Figure 9.14 illustrates the different flows available in OIDC:
Figure 9.14 – Authorization flows
Public clients, such as SPAs, historically relied on the Implicit Grant flow. However, due to its
security vulnerabilities, this flow is now deprecated and should be avoided. It may still be en -
countered in legacy applications. The recommended alternative for public clients is the Proof
Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) flow, which offers stronger protection by introducing a dynam -
ically generated secret to mitigate interception attacks. PKCE is used together with a secretless
Authorization Code flow.
For Model-View-Controller (MVC) applications, which are considered confidential clients, sev -
eral authorization flows are available. The Authorization Code flow relies on a pair of credentials
(client ID and client secret) that can be securely stored on the server side and, as its name indicates,
returns an authorization code to the client, which can then be exchanged for tokens.
Security Architecture 352
When an ID token is needed during the initial interaction with the authorization server, one option
is the Hybrid flow—a combination of the deprecated Implicit Grant and the Authorization Code
flow—or, preferably, the more secure PKCE in combination with the Authorization Code flow.
In short, the PKCE flow is recommended for all clients, whether public or confidential.
For machine-to-machine or service-to-service interactions, the most commonly used flow is the
Client Credentials flow. It relies on a pair of credentials—a client ID and a client secret—which is
appropriate for confidential clients. The flow is straightforward, involving a single HTTP request
to the token endpoint to obtain an access token.
A more secure variant uses a client ID in combination with a client certificate instead of a secret.
In this approach, the public key of the certificate must be uploaded to the application registered
in Entra ID. The client application then generates a client assertion—a JWT token signed with its
private key—to authenticate itself. This method is considered more secure because it leverages
asymmetric cryptography: the private key stays with the client, while only the public key is shared
with Entra ID, avoiding the risks associated with shared secrets. An even more secure version
of the Client Credentials flow is to use certificate-bound access tokens, which include certificate
information inside the token, but this is not supported by Entra.

90944.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90944.heading: Chapter 9 351
90944.content:
An additional machine-to-machine flow is Resource Owner Password Grant, which is discour -
aged but still used in situations where a resource does not support the Client Credentials flow
and the resource consumer does not have a human user. For example, the consumer could be a
background job that must interact with a resource with the equivalent of a service account. In
that case, the service account is like a user, but the username and password are used by a machine
instead of a human.
Lastly, the Device Code flow is designed for devices that do not have a browser or have very limited
UI capabilities. The device sends a request to Entra ID, waits for a code to display to the user, and
then repeatedly polls the token endpoint with the received code until the user is authenticated,
after which an access token is returned to the device.
You can easily watch this flow in action by sniffing the traffic of the az login --use-device-
code command.
Using PKCE for public clients is important, but it’s not the only consideration. You also need to
decide whether tokens should be returned directly to the client device. For years, SPAs and mobile
apps were typically designed to receive tokens directly from the authorization server. However, in
recent years, the BFF pattern—originally intended to serve client-specific needs—has emerged

90945.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90945.heading: Chapter 9 353
90945.content:
Chapter 9 353
as a preferred approach. It acts as an intermediary, helping to keep tokens off the client device
and enhancing security by limiting exposure.
Figure 9.15 illustrates the BFF pattern used for requesting and managing tokens on behalf of
client devices:
Figure 9.15 – BFF pattern with OIDC
Be aware that most application teams push back on this implementation as they see this as a
constraint. A potential trade-off consists of enforcing the BFF pattern for any internet-facing
asset and possibly allowing user tokens to surface in public clients for internal and corporate
apps. The risks encountered in letting tokens go back to the client are mostly linked to JavaS -
cript-based (cross-site scripting, etc.) and Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks. Note that while
the cookie-based approach protects against JavaScript-based attacks (providing the cookie is set
to HttpOnly), it does not protect against MITM.
Security Architecture 354
Scalability is another key consideration when implementing the BFF pattern. In a traditional setup
without a BFF, tokens are managed and stored locally on each client device, effectively distributing
the storage across all users. In contrast, introducing a BFF centralizes token management, requiring
server-side storage for all active sessions. This typically necessitates a distributed cache such as
Redis, along with proper session cleanup mechanisms. Additionally, placing a BFF between the
client and the target resource introduces extra latency. As with any architectural choice, adopting
BFF involves trade-offs between security, scalability, and performance.
Next, we’ll see how to perform proper token validation and clarify the role of scopes, which is
often misunderstood.
Getting up to speed with token validation and access control
mechanisms
Token validation is an important task that should be correctly understood.
There are two schools of thought: those who believe that relying solely on an API gateway without
additional validation in the backend code is sufficient, and those who believe the backend should
always validate the token, regardless of the architecture in place. I belong to the latter. I think it is
important to always validate the token in the code because the backend represents the resource
server. The gateway is useful to stop illegal requests earlier, but you should not rely only on the
gateway. Moreover, any change in the architecture could expose the backend.
However, by default, application code does not enforce any token validation. It is the responsibility
of developers to implement proper validation logic to ensure the received tokens are correctly
verified. In my experience conducting numerous API audits, I have consistently encountered se -
curity flaws—such as unprotected API operations or entire controllers lacking the proper access

90946.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90946.heading: Chapter 9 353
90946.content:
controls. Additionally, there is often a misunderstanding of what proper token validation looks like.
Figure 9.16 shows the different access control mechanisms that must be validated:

90947.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90947.heading: Chapter 9 355
90947.content:
Chapter 9 355
Figure 9.16 – Access control mechanisms
First and foremost, it’s important to understand that the structure and content of an access token
can vary depending on the authorization flow used to obtain it. An access token issued on behalf
of a user typically includes more claims than one obtained via the Client Credentials flow, which
represents an application-only context. Regardless of the flow or token format, certain elements
must always be validated systematically:
• The signature: The authorization server signs the token using its private key. To ensure its
authenticity, you must validate the signature using the corresponding public key, which
can be retrieved from the URL specified in the jwks_uri attribute found in the OIDC well-
known metadata endpoint. Relying solely on the token’s payload without verifying its
signature poses a serious security risk.
• The issuer: The iss claim represents the issuer. Checking this ensures the token was
generated by a trusted issuer.
Security Architecture 356
• The audience: The aud claim represents the audience(s), meaning the identifier of the
resource server(s). With this, you are sure that the client effectively requested a token to
talk to you.
• The expiration date: The exp claim represents the expiration date and time of the token.
Checking this ensures you do not let stale tokens go through.
• The not before claim: The nbf claim should ideally be verified as it represents the time
from which backends can process it.
It may also be useful to check the appid claim, which represents the identifier of the client appli -
cation used by the business service, if you want to restrict a backend to a given caller or a limited
set of callers. This can be particularly useful in server-to-server scenarios.
Beyond the basic validations, roles and scopes can also be leveraged—though they fulfill en -
tirely distinct functions. RBAC is applied by inspecting the role claim, which may include one
or more entries representing the roles defined by the resource server. These roles are injected
by Entra ID, either statically according to the client application’s registration or through user or
group assignments to the resource server’s application object, which links specific user groups
to designated roles.
For more advanced scenarios, RBAC might not be sufficient, and Attribute-Based Access Control
(ABAC) should be used instead. ABAC determines access based on a combination of attributes
that reflect business rules. ABAC often requires Claims Augmentation to inject additional claims
next to the default ones. For example, ABAC might be useful with rules such as this: Allow access
if the user is a French subscriber and has a gold-level subscription.
Next in line is the scope claim, which is often a source of confusion in OAuth 2.0. Many develop -

90948.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90948.heading: Chapter 9 355
90948.content:
ers tend to rely on scopes without deeper scrutiny—simply verifying their presence in a token to
allow API access. However, scopes should be treated as tools to define the boundaries of your APIs.
They enable the authorization server to clearly communicate to users that a client application
seeks to access specific features of a resource server on their behalf. This facilitates an informed
consent experience, empowering users to either approve or reject the requested access. A user
might have consented to the requested access, but it doesn’t mean the user actually has that
permission over the resource server. Here is a concrete example to clarify further: a marketplace
application may request the Microsoft Graph Sites.ReadWrite.All delegated permission, and
the user might consent to it, but the business service using the app should still be restricted to
the site collections the user has access to. In this case, SharePoint Online (the resource server)
validates the actual access of the user for which the token was requested and does not blindly
trust the Sites.ReadWrite.All scope injected by Entra ID in the token. The same considerations
apply to your own APIs.

90949.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90949.heading: Chapter 9 357
90949.content:
Chapter 9 357
That concludes our coverage of OIDC—now, let’s turn our attention to Privileged Access Man -
agement (PAM)and Enterprise Access Management (EAM).
Introducing PAM and red tenant architectures
PAM is a cybersecurity strategy and set of technologies designed to control, monitor, and secure
access to critical systems.
PAM helps minimize the risk of security breaches by enforcing the principle of least privilege,
providing just-in-time and just-enough access, auditing privileged actions, and isolating cre -
dentials in secure vaults.
At this stage, the Microsoft ecosystem provides a vaultless PAM model as there is no integrated
credential vault with password rotation and session isolation, which is why third parties such as
CyberArk and Thycotic are often used in addition to the Microsoft stack. Talking about these is
beyond the scope of this book, but be aware that they are the usual suspects in many companies.
Every serious organization has a PAM strategy that belongs to the broader Identity and Gover -
nance Administration (IGA) concept. However, the extent to which you implement a full-fledged
IGA or PAM, or something more basic, often depends on the industry and your risk appetite.
Implementing IGA is crucial for strengthening security, supporting regulatory compliance, and
boosting operational efficiency.
The core features of Entra ID’s IGA, made available by the Entra Suite plan, include user onboard -
ing and offboarding, policy-driven permission assignments through entitlement management,
and effective recertification via access reviews. Together, these capabilities strengthen the overall
PAM approach.
Now, let’s explore Enhanced Security Admin Environment (ESAE) and Enterprise Access Model
(EAM), which are PAM-friendly architectures.
Microsoft introduced the concept of red forest about a decade ago, which targeted Active Directory
and mostly focused on on-premises environments. Red forest is part of the ESAE practice. The
red forest concept relies on the following tiers:
• Tier 0: This tier represents the crown jewels of your identity assets. Systems such as Active
Directory Domain Services (AD DS), Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), AD FS, Privileged
Access Workstation (PAW), and highly privileged accounts (for example, domain admin),
are part of Tier 0. In the red forest architecture, this tier is fully managed by a separate
Active Directory. Administrators receive PAWs to perform their administrative work and
use another regular device for non-administrative work, such as writing docs and col -
laborating with others.
Security Architecture 358
• Tier 1: This tier includes member servers (application servers, SQL servers, and so on),
as well as the server admin accounts. It basically includes all the servers except those
belonging to tier 0.

90950.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90950.heading: Chapter 9 357
90950.content:
• Tier 2: This tier includes user workstations and help desk support tools, as well as ac -
counts needed to manage tier 2 assets. Tier 2 accounts cannot access tier 1 or tier 0 assets.
While ESAE is now considered legacy—though still in use—it has been succeeded by EAM, which
has become the standard for modern and cloud-native environments since around 2020. EAM
builds on some of ESAE’s foundational principles, such as the tiered architecture, but redefines
the tiers based on logical boundaries such as the control plane (former tier 0), management
plane, and data/workload plane (former tier 1), as well as user access and app access (former tier
2). Despite the shift in structure, EAM shares the same objective as ESAE: to uphold the principle
of least privilege and enforce strong governance over all high-privilege activities. Another key
distinction between EAM and ESAE is that in EAM, high-privilege admin accounts reside strictly
within the control plane, and the zero-trust security model is strictly enforced using CAPs.
While EAM is not prescriptive about using a single- or multi-tenant approach, an emerging trend
consists of using a separate red tenant to control and manage all control plane assets. Red tenant
admin users leverage Entra ID’s cross-tenant access capabilities to gain access to the blue tenant
(workforce/resource tenant), where roles are effectively granted. Using separate tenants enforces
stronger isolation between the control plane and the other layers, as well as dependencies. For
example, the Intune admin in the workforce tenant only exists in that tenant, and as such is fully
isolated from the red tenant. It also allows us to make sure PAWs can only be used by red tenant
users, and the workforce tenant would block any office user using regular machines to perform
administration tasks using CAPs. Admin users typically log in to PAWs using strong authentica -
tion mechanisms, such as FIDO2 keys, and receive their privileges (just in time and just enough)
through a PIM session.
Figure 9.17 illustrates what EAM may look like using a red tenant:

90951.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90951.heading: Chapter 9 359
90951.content:
Chapter 9 359
Figure 9.17 – Example of what EAM with red tenant may look like
It is important to understand that there is no definitive rule for determining which service be -
longs to which layer. Figure 9.17 illustrates a sample set of Azure services categorized under the
workload/data plane; however, this is by no means exhaustive. As a general guideline, any service
that hosts data or runs workloads is considered part of the workload/data plane. Services that
support the operation and administration of the environment fall under the management plane.
Components enabling user and application access are part of the user and app access layer. The
red tenant is strictly limited to core identity services and is responsible for managing highly
privileged accounts.
Security Architecture 360
However, as is often the case, putting theory into practice can be challenging. In Figure 9.17, a clear
tension emerges: Microsoft Intune is included in the red tenant to manage and enforce controls
on PAWs. While Intune is theoretically part of the management plane, the red tenant is intended
to be strictly limited to control plane assets. This represents a necessary deviation from the mod -
el, as PAWs cannot reasonably be managed by an Intune instance residing in a different tenant.
While the use of PAWs enhances security, it can be seen as a logistical and financial burden—par -
ticularly at scale—since it often involves provisioning and managing multiple physical devices per
administrator. It also means that administrators may need to carry two separate devices when
commuting, which can be inconvenient.
As a potential alternative—albeit with a lower security posture—a Virtual Privileged Access
Workstation (VPAW) restricted to red tenant users only and hosted on Azure Virtual Desktop
can serve as a more flexible solution.
The company glueckkanja has an Azure Marketplace product called Managed Red Tenant that
is moving in that direction, which may be worth evaluating depending on your organization’s
needs and risk tolerance.
For additional information on PAM, you can read some of the online documentation: https://
learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security/privileged-access-workstations/privileged-
access-access-model.
Zooming in on CSPM
CSPM is a proactive approach that consists of continuously assessing the security posture of an
environment. CSPM ensures the overall configuration adheres to the best security practices. Any
deviation is flagged, and recommendations are made to remediate non-compliant resources.
Figure 9.18 shows the different built-in tools that help ensure a proper security posture in Azure:

90952.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90952.heading: Chapter 9 361

90953.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90953.heading: Chapter 9 363
90953.content:
Chapter 9 363
This policy essentially verifies whether the Microsoft.Sql/servers/publicNetworkAccess prop -
erty is set to Disabled. If it’s not, the policy enforces compliance by setting it to Disabled using
the Modify effect. While this approach is practical—since it automatically corrects non-compliant
configurations rather than blocking them—it can conflict with stateful infrastructure-as-code
or GitOps-based tools such as Terraform or Argo CD, potentially leading to deployment issues
later on. If you’re using such tools, it’s recommended to use the Deny effect instead. This ensures
that deployments are compliant from the outset, avoiding hidden drifts and conflicts caused by
automatic modifications. The rule engine is very powerful and allows you to evaluate nearly any
resource attribute. Azure has hundreds of built-in policies and lets you build your own.
Beyond just controlling deployments, policies continuously assess the entire environment and
provide insights, as well as tools such as remediation tasks to restore compliance.
You can visit this link to find hundreds of policy examples: https://github.com/Azure/azure-
policy.
Exploring Foundational and Defender CSPM plans
The Foundational CSPM (free tier) is a multi-cloud solution that adds a layer of intelligence,
visibility, and context on top of Azure Policy. It comes with features such as the secure score and
actionable recommendations about what you should do to fix some security issues. Figure 9.19
shows the secure score that is calculated by Foundational CSPM:
Figure 9.19 – Secure score in Foundational CSPM
Foundational CSPM provides many recommendations of different types. Figure 9.20 shows rec -
ommendations related to storage accounts:
Figure 9.20 – CSPM recommendation
Security Architecture 364
When you click on a specific recommendation, you’re either given the option to fix it immediately
or provided with guidance on how to resolve the issue.
Figure 9.21 – CSPM remediation example
While it might be tempting to click the Fix button, you should always assess the cost impact
before doing so. Moreover, this could conflict with your infrastructure-as-code practice, so you
should include the fix in the next infrastructure-as-code release.
You may encounter hundreds of recommendations, depending on the overall state of your envi -
ronment. However, Foundational CSPM does not evaluate risk factors or the possible attack paths
since it is only made available by Defender CSPM.
Defender CSPM essentially identifies possible attack paths and maps them to the MITRE ATT&CK
framework, a well-known classification of cyberattacks and intrusions. There is a significant
difference between the two plans, and you can evaluate them in detail by reviewing the informa -
tion available at this link: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/

90954.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90954.heading: Chapter 9 363
90954.content:
concept-cloud-security-posture-management.
One interesting feature, among others, that is part of Defender CSPM is Microsoft Defender Ex -
ternal Attack Surface Management (EASM).
It’s a specialized offering designed to assess all your existing externally facing assets. It scans
your domains, certificates, and open ports, then provides a detailed report with findings and
actionable recommendations for remediation. It also provides visibility into assets you may have
overlooked or forgotten to decommission, helping reduce unnecessary exposure and optimize
resource management.

90955.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90955.heading: Chapter 9 365
90955.content:
Chapter 9 365
Finally, another notable capability is Defender for DevOps, which is part of Defender CSPM. It
connects your Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) tools to Azure, providing a unified view
for end-to-end CSPM visibility and oversight across your development and deployment processes.
Zooming in on CWPP
CSPM and CWPP are closely related, but the key distinction lies in their focus: CSPM takes a
proactive approach by continuously evaluating security posture and configurations to prevent
attacks, whereas CWPP focuses on threat detection at runtime.
In Azure, Microsoft Defender for Cloud is the cornerstone of CWPP, along with other Defender
options. Figure 9.22 shows the most commonly used options:
Figure 9.22 – CWPP most common options
Figure 9.22 illustrates the granularity of Defender, allowing you to enable all features or selectively
activate only those deemed most critical. Billing is generally based on the specific plans enabled
and the number of protected resources.
Security Architecture 366
All Defender variants integrate directly with Microsoft XDR or Sentinel—tools used to support
SecOps activities, which we will cover later in this chapter. In addition, most Defender offerings
also contribute to CSPM by providing proactive recommendations to further harden the protected
services. Defender sends both signals and security alerts to XDR or Sentinel, which are used to
analyze and respond to security incidents.
Microsoft Defender for Identity primarily covers Active Directory and AD FS to identify and detect
threats against these on-premises infrastructures.
Defender for Resource Manager focuses on interactions with the Azure Resource Manager (ARM)
API, which includes any action performed with the Azure portal, the Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell,
and infrastructure as code. It can detect anomalies such as impossible travel (for example, an
action from the US at 9 a.m. followed by another from France an hour later), the use of exploit
toolkits, and malicious virtual machine extensions.
Defender for Databases is centered around SQL Server (all forms: Azure SQL, SQL Managed In -
stance, and self-hosted SQL servers), Cosmos DB, as well as other relational database engines. It
protects against SQL injections, access from unusual data centers, brute-force attacks, and so on.
Defender for APIs is particularly valuable given the central role of APIs in modern architectures.
It detects anomalies such as unusual spikes in API usage or irregular payload sizes by comparing
them to baseline traffic patterns. It also checks whether the API endpoints are subject to authori -
zation. Additionally, it can classify the types of data handled by your APIs, helping you understand
what is exposed to consumers.
Defender for AI helps protect against prompt injections, wallet attacks, and the exposure of sensi -

90956.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90956.heading: Chapter 9 365
90956.content:
tive data to LLMs, among other things. Wallet attacks, in particular, can be mitigated using the AI
Gateway pattern discussed in Chapter 8, Artificial Intelligence Architecture . Enabling Defender for
APIs on an API that shields the LLM using the AI Gateway pattern can be effective, not because of
Defender’s features themselves, but because the LLM stays hidden while the proxy API is protected.
Both Defender for Storage and Defender for Endpoint offer malware protection, but Defender for
Endpoint provides much broader coverage for virtual machines, with the ability to detect a wide
range of threats occurring within those environments. Needless to say that Defender for Storage is
particularly interesting when using Azure Storage’s SFTP feature. Blobs are tagged once scanned,
and the scan results can be captured using Event Grid for further actions. Note that at this stage,
Defender for Storage does not use sandboxing, which is a way to execute suspicious files into an
isolated environment, enabling advanced threat protection.

90957.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90957.heading: Chapter 9 367
90957.content:
Chapter 9 367
Defender for Containers protects against reconnaissance activities, lateral movements, and cryp -
to-mining, among other things. Additionally, Defender for Containers performs container image
scanning, including daily re-scans. Microsoft has written a simulation script that generates at -
tacks from within an AKS cluster. The script is available here: https://raw.githubusercontent.
com/microsoft/Defender-for-Cloud-Attack-Simulation/refs/heads/main/simulation.py.
Defender for DNS should move to Defender for Servers with the same protection coverage. It
protects against communication with malicious DNS resolvers and malicious domains, anom -
alous protocols, and network patterns. A threat that Defender for DNS cannot detect on its own
is the so-called dangling DNS, which occurs when a malicious party takes over a subdomain. In
short, if you have a web app hosted at a subdomain such as contoso.azurewebsites.net and
a corresponding CNAME record in your DNS, deleting the app without removing the CNAME
leaves a vulnerability. A malicious actor could register a new App Service with the same sub -
domain, effectively hijacking your DNS entry, which makes you lose control over the content of
the subdomain. Defender for App Service helps mitigate as it includes dangling DNS detection.
Although using Azure Firewall as a DNS proxy isn’t strictly part of workload protection, it remains
a valuable complementary approach for routing DNS traffic through Azure Firewall.
Given the fast-paced evolution of the Defender ecosystem, it’s important to regularly reassess its
capabilities when defining and implementing a CWPP strategy.
You can visit the following link for a comprehensive view of the security alerts generated by the
various Defender options: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/
alerts-reference.
It’s worth noting that investing in CSPM is far more effective than relying solely on CWPP. CSPM
takes a proactive approach by continuously verifying that security best practices are enforced
across your environments, helping to prevent cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities. CWPP
serves as a complementary layer, but it should not be your only line of defense.
Zooming in on DevSecOps
Because CI/CD was already introduced in Chapter 2, Solution Architecture, this section will focus
exclusively on security practices.
The purpose of DevSecOps is to integrate security practices into the DevOps or GitOps process. It
is based on the shift-left principle, which consists of shifting some responsibilities to development
teams and making sure to tackle security concerns as early as possible in the development life cycle.
Security Architecture 368
DevOps and GitOps both heavily rely on automation. As mentioned in the introduction, security
teams often operate in silos, with approval processes relying on tickets and occurring outside the

90958.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90958.heading: Chapter 9 367
90958.content:
DevOps pipeline. The core objective of DevSecOps is to break down these barriers by embedding
security checks and approvals directly into the automation workflow.
The most effective way to achieve this is by involving security analysts directly in the CI/CD
approval process. This means having them participate in peer reviews and approve or reject
security-related changes through pull requests. To streamline this workflow, quality gates can
be established to ensure that no solution is promoted to higher environments until it meets the
required security and compliance standards.
Figure 9.23 shows different tools and DevSecOps practices that should be enforced in any orga -
nization:
Figure 9.23 – DevSecOps
The shift-left principle involves conducting early security checks in the development life cycle,
primarily through Software Composition Analysis (SCA) and SAST. Both techniques analyze
source code to detect potential vulnerabilities and provide remediation guidance. These scans
are typically integrated into build pipelines to catch issues before deployment. They generate
reports that typically include severity ratings or risk levels that can be used to define quality gates.

90959.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90959.heading: Chapter 9 369
90959.content:
Chapter 9 369
In practice, these reports are often overlooked unless strict quality gates are enforced. Apart from
tools like PSRules that scan IaC artefacts, Azure does not provide native SAST or SCA frameworks.
Third-party tools such as Snyk and AppScan can be integrated to fill this gap. Snyk, in particular,
offers strong capabilities for scanning container images—an essential complement to source
code analysis to ensure end-to-end security.
Once the code is built and meets the required quality standards, it should be deployed. Ideally,
DAST tools and a strong CSPM solution should be integrated from the development environment
onward. This enables early detection of runtime vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, reinforcing
security throughout the application life cycle. As we have seen in the Zooming in on CSPM sec -
tion, only Azure Policy and the Foundational plan of Defender are already impressive from that
perspective. For AKS-hosted workloads, policies are defined in Azure Policy and enforced by the
Gatekeeper admission controller, ensuring deployments are compliant with security best practices.
For those willing to go the extra mile, enabling runtime protection from the development envi -
ronment provides enhanced visibility into potential live threats as workloads run. In the Azure
ecosystem, this can be achieved through Defender for Cloud workload protection, with Defender
for Containers offering specialized coverage for containerized environments, as we have seen
in our Zooming in on CWPP section. An alternative, though not mutually exclusive, is to rely on
Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) to further strengthen the security level of appli -
cations through context-aware agents, but this practice is not common and is often overkill if all
the other tools mentioned in this section are already in use.
Lastly, Defender for DevOps is yet another option that lets you plug Defender into your SDLC
solutions (GitHub and Azure DevOps for now). Once onboarded, Defender will scan both the
infrastructure code and the entire repositories and pipelines, providing not only code recom -
mendations but also insights for the DevOps environments themselves.
Let’s now look at security operations, also known as SecOps.
Zooming in on SecOps
At the very end of the application life cycle comes SecOps, which is a practice aimed at detecting,
responding to, and mitigating security threats. The primary purpose of SecOps is to continuous -
ly monitor the live environment. We leverage CSPM upstream as a way to proactively prevent
misconfigurations and vulnerabilities, and CWPP and SecOps downstream to monitor the live
environment, as well as to generate and handle security incidents.
Security Architecture 370
Figure 9.24 depicts the SecOps landscape in Azure:

90960.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90960.heading: Chapter 9 369
90960.content:
Figure 9.24 – SecOps landscape in Azure
Extended Detection and Response (XDR) is ensured by Microsoft XDR, a unified solution that
correlates signals coming from all the Defender products. Its portal is the one-stop shop for every
SecOps team member, as it also integrates Azure Sentinel.
However, Sentinel is still considered a SIEM/SOAR solution, used to connect various data sources
to ingest log data and receive security incidents generated by Defender. The logical sequence to
ingest and work with data in Sentinel is shown in Figure 9.25.
Figure 9.25 – Sentinel configuration sequence
Once you install a provider using Content Hub, you can configure its corresponding data connec -
tor(s) to ingest the data you want to retrieve. Each provider comes with a default set of analytic
rules and playbooks, which help you analyze and react to ingested data.

90961.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90961.heading: Chapter 9 371
90961.content:
Chapter 9 371
There are two types of rules, both written in KQL: scheduled and Near-Real-Time (NRT). NRT
rules provide up-to-the-minute threat detection but are currently limited to 50 per customer,
which means that you should carefully select rules for which you consider an immediate detec -
tion and response should be given.
Data is ingested into Log Analytics, and it is considered best practice to work with a dedicated
workspace for Sentinel.
The volume of ingested data can be substantial, potentially resulting in high ingestion costs. It’s
important to carefully choose only the data sources that are truly relevant to your environment.
Additionally, consider setting a daily cap on the Log Analytics workspace to avoid unexpected
cost overruns—especially in non-production environments.
One of the key data sources commonly integrated with Microsoft Sentinel is Entra ID. It provides
valuable insights to detect credential-based attacks such as password spraying and credential
stuffing, as well as anomalies in credential usage. To fully benefit from this data source, you must
have at least a P1 or P2 Entra ID license.
Another essential data source when using virtual machines (IaaS) is Defender for Servers, espe -
cially when combined with Defender for Endpoint and other virtual machine-specific protection
mechanisms. Since the attack surface of virtual machines is typically broader than that of PaaS
services, it’s crucial to enable these Defender solutions and ingest their data and alerts into Sen -
tinel to gain a comprehensive view of your infrastructure’s security posture.
Responding to incidents involves automation rules that allow the automatic assignment of an
owner, a tag, a severity, and to respond with concrete actions using playbooks.
Playbooks are based on Logic Apps workflows, which give you all the flexibility in terms of how
you want to handle and respond to an incident.
The challenge with Sentinel is finding the right balance between noise—too many false positives—
and silence—actual threats not being detected and handled. Setting up Sentinel and connecting
data sources can be done in minutes, but the actual work resides in the setup of analytical rules and
playbooks. Additionally, SecOps team members should connect to the XDR portal on a daily basis.
Third-party solutions such as Splunk and QRadar are also commonly used in SOAR/SIEM and
broader SecOps scenarios. In such cases, they are typically integrated with Azure Event Hubs to
ingest logs and perform detection and response activities accordingly.
Security Architecture 372
Zooming in on appliances and CASB solutions
Figure 9.26 shows the common technologies used as appliances and CASB solutions in Azure:
Figure 9.26 – Appliances and CASB solutions
We previously introduced the concepts of WAFs and next-generation firewalls in Chapter 3, In -

90962.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90962.heading: Chapter 9 371
90962.content:
frastructure Design, without exploring them in depth. In this section, we’ll delve into Azure WAF
policies and Azure Firewall. It is important to note that many organizations opt for third-party
solutions—such as F5, Imperva, or Cloudflare for WAF capabilities, and Palo Alto, Fortinet, or
Check Point for firewalls. A layered approach is also common, for example, using Cloudflare as
the global entry point and Application Gateway with WAF policies as a secondary WAF, offering
an additional layer of protection. Let’s further explore WAF policies.
Diving deeper into WAF policies
Azure WAF policies consist of both managed rules and custom rules. These policies can be asso -
ciated with either Azure Front Door (serving as a global WAF) or Application Gateway (acting as
a regional WAF). Each policy can operate in either prevention mode, where malicious requests
are blocked, or detection mode, where traffic is monitored but not actively blocked.

90963.title: azurecloudnativearchitecturemapbooksecondedition
90963.heading: Chapter 9 373
90963.content:
Chapter 9 373
A recommended best practice is to enable WAF policies in detection mode early in the development
life cycle. This allows teams to review WAF logs, identify potential policy violations, and provide
actionable feedback to development teams. However, in practice, WAF logs are often overlooked,
which can result in unexpected disruptions when switching to prevention mode—potentially
causing applications to malfunction. Continuous monitoring of WAF violations is essential, as
false positives can occur and may lead to legitimate traffic being blocked unnecessarily.
Multiple manage rulesets are available, as shown in Figure 9.27:
Figure 9.27 – Managed rulesets (truncated)
Security Architecture 374
Azure WAF provides two rulesets designed to protect against the well-known Open Worldwide
Application Security Project (OWASP) threats and attacks, along with an additional Micro -
soft-specific ruleset. Each rule can be fully enabled or disabled, and fine-grained exclusions allow
specific parts of a request to be ignored, helping to reduce false positives. A WAF policy can be
associated with different scopes within Application Gateway—globally at the gateway level
(applying to all applications), at the listener level, or per path-based rule. More specific scopes
take precedence over the broader scope. This granularity offers significant flexibility to tailor WAF
policies to the specific needs of each application. You may have a gateway-level policy applying
defaults that you absolutely want to enforce, and more application-specific policies that would ac -
commodate application-specific requirements. WAF policies can also inherit from parent policies.
Figure 9.28 shows a WAF policy attached to a specific listener:
Figure 9.28 – WAF policy attached to a specific listener
When enabled in prevention mode, any attempt to perform a malicious request will result in a
403 Forbidden error, as shown by Figure 9.29:
Figure 9.29 – WAF policy in action

90964.heading: Chapter 9 375
90964.content:

custom rules, such as the one shown in Figure 9.30.
Figure 9.30 – Allow only callers from Belgium
This rule will block any non-Belgium calling client. We can have more advanced rules, including
multiple logical operators.
Security Architecture 376
To see the WAF logs, we must enable a diagnostic setting at the level of Application Gateway (or
Front Door) itself, as shown in Figure 9.31:
Figure 9.31 – Enabling WAF logs
Once enabled, logs will be stored in Log Analytics for further investigation. As highlighted earlier,
you should enable WAF logs in development and have someone looking at the logs. To efficiently

let detectedRequests = AGWFirewallLogs
| where RuleId == "949110"
| project TransactionId, TimeGenerated, ClientIp, RequestUri,
Hostname;
AGWFirewallLogs
| join kind= inner (detectedRequests) on TransactionId
| where RuleId != "949110"
| project TimeGenerated, ClientIp, RequestUri, Hostname, RuleId, Message,

90965.content:
